parts: Hold out your left hand.
Look at the finger next to the little one.
Millions of people put a wedding ring on that finger.
And for centuries, they said they had a reason.
They believed a vein ran from that finger straight to your heart.
It is a lovely idea.
Is it true?
And if it is not, why is the ring still there?
Five explanations.
One is a medical claim.
One is a church ritual.
One is a guess that science can test.
One depends on which country you live in.
And one is hidden in the finger's own name.
Which of them is real?
Here are the rules.
For each explanation, we look at the paper trail.
Names.
Dates.
Books.
Then we stamp it.
Documented means the records exist.
Disputed means experts still argue, or the evidence is thin.
Myth means the evidence says no.
And when a conclusion is ours and not a historian's, we call it our reading.
Let's start with the heart.
Case one. The heart.
Our oldest source is Roman.
In the second century, a writer named Aulus Gellius jotted down a note about rings.
He says he has heard that the ancient Greeks wore a ring on the left hand.
On the finger next to the little one.
And that Romans commonly did the same.
Not a wedding ring. Just a ring.
Then Gellius gives the reason.
A writer named Apion, in a history of Egypt, said that Egyptians had cut open human bodies.
They found a very fine nerve, running from that finger alone to the heart.
Gellius is only passing on what Apion wrote.
A nerve. Not a vein. Remember that word.
We found no Egyptian text that says this.
Around the year four hundred, the Roman writer Macrobius repeats the nerve.
In the seventh century, Isidore of Seville writes that a vein links that finger to the heart, something the ancients thought worth noting.
The nerve has become a vein.
Now ask where the famous Latin name comes from.
Vena amoris. The vein of love.
The earliest user we found is an English lawyer, Henry Swinburne.
He wrote it in his lifetime. It was printed in sixteen eighty-six, long after he died.
So the vein of love is not an old Roman phrase.
As far as we found, it is much younger.
Now the evidence.
In sixteen twenty-eight, William Harvey described how blood circulates through the body.
After that, anyone could check where blood really goes.
In sixteen forty-six, the physician Thomas Browne published a book of popular errors.
He lists the old reasons for this finger, one by one.
Then he writes that inspection does not confirm a special vessel in it.
Today, an anatomy teaching site says it plainly.
There is no single vein linking one finger straight to the heart.
Verdict.
The custom is documented.
The belief is documented.
The vein of love is a myth.
Case two. The church.
In medieval southern England, many weddings followed the Sarum rite.
The groom touches the bride's thumb with the ring. In the name of the Father.
Then the next finger. And of the Son.
Then the next. And of the Holy Ghost.
On the ring finger he says Amen. The ring rests there.
And the book gives a reason.
Medicine teaches, it says, that a certain vein in that finger reaches the heart.
So the Trinity count does not replace the vein.
It leads to it.
The English Book of Common Prayer fixed the rule in writing in the sixteenth century.
The ring goes on the fourth finger of the woman's left hand.
The edition of sixteen sixty-two still says so.
Verdict.
The ritual is documented.
But it explains how the ring got there, not why that finger was chosen.
Case three. The practical finger.
Browne lists another old reason, and credits it to Macrobius.
The right hand did most of the work, so the ring went on the left.
And the fourth finger is the least used, and guarded on both sides.
Can we test that? Only one piece.
In two thousand, a study in the Journal of Neuroscience measured how independently people can move each finger.
The ring finger was the least independent of the five. That is not the same as least used.
Try it.
Lay your hand flat. Lift only the ring finger.
It tends to drag a neighbour along.
Our reading: a finger that is hard to move is a quiet place for a ring.
It would get in the way less.
But no ancient document we found says that is why the Greeks picked it.
Verdict.
Disputed.
It fits. It is not proven.
Case four. Is it the same everywhere?
No.
In Russia, Poland and Bulgaria, the wedding ring goes on the right hand.
So it does in Eastern Orthodox weddings.
In the Netherlands, tradition split by church. Traditionally, Catholics on the left. Protestants on the right.
In a traditional Jewish ceremony, the ring goes on the bride's right index finger during the ceremony.
Browne says even the ancient Gauls and Britons wore rings on the middle finger.
Our reading: cultures that chose another finger did fine without the vein.
A body does not change at the border.
A custom does.
Verdict.
That the left ring finger is the one natural choice is a myth.
Case five. The name of the finger.
So far, our reasons were about rings and hearts.
This one is about medicine.
Doctors have a Latin name for the ring finger.
Digitus medicinalis. The medicine finger.
Why?
Isidore of Seville, in the seventh century, says doctors used it to collect medicinal powders.
One translation says doctors used it to apply ointments.
We only read Isidore through later writers.
Another answer is the vein itself.
Macrobius is the writer who repeated the nerve.
In his book, a doctor explains the vein to the other guests at a banquet.
Even the text admits doubt: an idle tale, or a true explanation?
A third idea is more modern.
In nineteen ninety, Magyar read the finger's names as a sign of an old belief that it was magical.
Wikipedia reports it. We could not open the original.
Then there is the plainest answer.
The other Latin name is anularis. The ring finger.
Isidore says it is called that because we wear a ring on it.
Our reading: the name may follow the custom, not cause it.
Verdict.
The names are documented.
The reasons are disputed.
So what do we really know?
Romans wrote that people wore rings on that finger. Documented.
The medieval Sarum rite wrote the vein into the wedding service. Documented.
The English prayer book fixed the finger in writing in the sixteenth century. Documented.
The finger has old names. Documented. Why? Disputed.
The vein itself? Myth.
The one natural finger? Myth.
The practical reason? Disputed.
And why did anyone pick that finger first?
A reference work says the origin is not definitively known.
That question stays open.
Our reading: two old habits met on one finger.
A ring on that finger. And a ring for marriage.
Then the reasons kept changing.
A nerve. A vein. A Trinity count. A prayer book. A name.
The finger never moved.
A custom can outlive every reason ever given for it.
A ring is a promise you can see.
Here is another small thing you see every day, and rarely question.
Why does almost everything you buy carry a pattern of black stripes?
